items.prose: A check screens 1,000 trades a day for fat-finger errors, and about 2 are errors. It runs at $\alpha = 0.02$ and $\beta = 0.10$. A false alarm costs £15 of a trader's time. A missed error costs £8,000.
items.question: What is the expected cost per day, in £?

feedback.correct: £299.40 in false alarms plus £1,600 in misses: £1,899.40.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the false-alarm cost on 998 good trades and the miss cost on 2 errors.

byKey.alarms-only: That is only the false alarms. Add $0.10 \times 2 \times 8{,}000$ for missed errors.
byKey.misses-only: That is only the misses. Add $0.02 \times 998 \times 15$ for false alarms.
byKey.all-trades: You applied $\alpha$ to all 1,000 trades and left out the misses.

explain.text: False alarms: $0.02 \times 998 \times 15 = 299.40$. Misses: $0.10 \times 2 \times 8{,}000 = 1{,}600$. Here misses dominate, so loosening the cut-off to cut $\beta$ would probably pay.

items.prose: A test at $\alpha = 0.01$, one-sided, should have 90% power, so $z_\alpha = 2.326$ and $z_\beta = 1.282$. The effect is a quarter of an sd: $\delta/\sigma = 0.25$.
items.question: How many observations are needed? Round up.

byKey.no-zbeta: You left out $z_\beta$, which gives only 50% power.
byKey.default: That uses 6.18, the constant for 5% and 80%. Here the constant is $3.608^2 = 13.02$.
byKey.down: 208 observations fall just short of 90% power. Round up.

explain.text: $(2.326 + 1.282)^2 = 13.02$, and $(\sigma/\delta)^2 = 16$, so $n = 208.3$, rounded up to 209. The stricter test and higher power cost more than twice the 99 needed at 5% and 80%.

items.prose: We derive the sample size for a one-sided $z$ test with power $1 - \beta$, where $\Phi(z_\beta) = 1 - \beta$.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: We need $\Phi\left(\dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma} - z_\alpha\right) = 1 - \beta$: the power formula set to the target
$\dfrac{\delta\sqrt n}{\sigma} - z_\alpha = z_\beta$: $\Phi$ is increasing, and $\Phi(z_\beta) = 1 - \beta$
$\sqrt n = \dfrac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\delta}$: add $z_\alpha$, then multiply by $\sigma/\delta$
$n = \left(\dfrac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\delta}\right)^2$: square both sides, both positive

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line undoes one operation on $n$.

byKey.s2: Removing $\Phi$ needs the target equation first.

explain.text: Removing $\Phi$ is allowed because it is strictly increasing, so equal values mean equal arguments. With $z_\alpha = 1.645$ and $z_\beta = 0.842$ the constant is $2.487^2 = 6.18$.

items.prose: In data-mined signals, 2% are real. A test with power 0.9 at $\alpha = 0.05$ passes a signal. An independent replication on new data also passes it.
items.question: What is $P(\text{real} \mid \text{both pass})$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each pass multiplies the odds by $0.9/0.05 = 18$.

byKey.single: 0.269 is after one pass. The replication multiplies the odds by 18 again.
byKey.one-minus-alpha-sq: You read $1 - 0.05^2$ as the chance it is real. That ignores the 2% base rate.
byKey.power-sq: 0.81 is the chance a real signal passes twice, the reverse of what is asked.

explain.text: Prior odds $2{:}98 = 1{:}49$. Each independent pass multiplies by 18: $324{:}49$, so $P = 324/373 = 0.869$. One pass gives only 0.269, which is why replication on fresh data matters.

items.title: A paired test in code

items.question: Complete `paired_t(x, y)`.

widget.starter:

def paired_t(x, y):

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: four compared with `math.isclose` against scipy.stats.ttest_rel, one expecting ValueError. NumPy and SciPy are available but load slowly; this task needs only `math`.

feedback.correct: Your function matches SciPy's paired test.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Work on the differences, use $n - 1$ in the sd, and check the lengths first.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace the `...` with the body.

explain.text:
On the lesson's algorithm data it returns 3.80. Checking lengths first matters, because `zip` silently drops the extra items and would give a wrong answer.

```python
if len(x) != len(y):
    raise ValueError("x and y must pair up")
d = [a - b for a, b in zip(x, y)]
```

items.prose: A quant tests 50 strategies a year on 2 years (504 days) of data each. 10% have a true Sharpe ratio of 1, so a daily mean of $1/\sqrt{252} = 0.063$ sd. The rest have none. Each test is one-sided at 5%. Use $\Phi(-0.231) = 0.409$.
items.question: Of the strategies that pass, what share have a real edge?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the power first: shift $= 0.063 \times \sqrt{504} = 1.414$.

byKey.power: 0.409 is the power, the share of real strategies that pass. You want the share of passes that are real.
byKey.full-power: That assumes 80% power. With two years of data the power is only 0.409.
byKey.one-minus-alpha: 0.95 is $1 - \alpha$, the chance a dud fails. Weigh the passes by the base rate.

explain.text: Shift $= \sqrt{504/252} = 1.414$, so power $= \Phi(1.414 - 1.645) = 0.409$. Real passes: $0.1 \times 0.409 = 0.0409$; false passes: $0.9 \times 0.05 = 0.045$. Fewer than half the passes are real, because two years cannot reliably detect a Sharpe of 1.

items.title: Two desks, one quarter
items.prompt: Over one quarter of 60 days, desk A made a mean £12,400 a day, with sd £41,000. Desk B made £3,100 a day, with sd £28,000. Tested against zero, A has $p = 0.023$ and B has $p = 0.39$. (a) Test whether the desks' means differ, two-sided at 5%, and state your decision. (b) Explain why the two separate $p$-values do not settle the question. (c) Suppose the true gap is £9,300 a day. How many days per desk give 80% power at 5% two-sided? Use the normal approximation. (d) Give a 95% confidence interval for the gap. Name one assumption of the test that daily P&L may break.
items.model:
**(a)** The two desks are separate samples, so we use Welch's statistic.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{SE} &= \sqrt{\frac{41{,}000^2}{60} + \frac{28{,}000^2}{60}} \\ &= \sqrt{28.02\text{m} + 13.07\text{m}} \\ &= \sqrt{41.08\text{m}} \approx 6{,}410. \end{aligned}$$
Then $t = (12{,}400 - 3{,}100)/6{,}410 = 1.45$. Welch's degrees of freedom are about 104, so the two-sided 5% critical value is 1.98. Since $1.45 < 1.98$ we do not reject $H_0$: equal means. The two-sided $p$ is 0.15.

**(b)** A's $p = 0.023$ and B's $p = 0.39$ each test a desk against zero. Neither tests A against B. A's mean could sit just above the line and B's just below, with almost no gap between them. Only the test of the gap, in (a), compares the desks, and it is not significant.

**(c)** For a two-sided 5% test with 80% power, the gap must sit $z_{0.025} + z_{0.2} = 1.96 + 0.842 = 2.802$ standard errors from 0. With $n$ days each, $\text{SE} = \sqrt{(41{,}000^2 + 28{,}000^2)/n} = 49{,}649/\sqrt n$. So
$$\begin{aligned} \frac{9{,}300\sqrt n}{49{,}649} &= 2.802 \\ \Rightarrow \sqrt n &= 14.96 \\ \Rightarrow n &\approx 224 \text{ days each}. \end{aligned}$$
That is almost four quarters, not one.

**(d)** The 95% interval for the gap is $9{,}300 \pm 1.98 \times 6{,}410$, about $-\text{£}3{,}400$ to $\text{£}22{,}000$ a day. That is the honest summary: A may be far better, or slightly worse. The test assumes independent days. Daily P&L is often autocorrelated, and both desks may share market days, so the true SE could be larger. If the desks trade the same days, a paired analysis of daily differences would be fairer.

rubric.text: Computes SE $\approx \text{£}6{,}410$ and $t \approx 1.45$ with Welch's formula.
Compares with a critical value near 1.98 (or $p \approx 0.15$) and does not reject equal means.
Explains that each $p$ tests a desk against zero, and that only the test of the gap compares the desks.
Sets $9{,}300\sqrt n/49{,}649 = 1.96 + 0.842$ and finds about 224 days each.
Gives the interval of roughly $-\text{£}3{,}400$ to $\text{£}22{,}000$ and reads it correctly.
Names independence of days (autocorrelation or shared market days) as an assumption that may fail.

items.prose: A factor paper's abstract says: “Our signal is significant at $p = 0.004$, so there is a 99.6% chance it is real. We tried 40 specifications and report the best.”
items.question: Which criticisms are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: 99.6% reads $1 - p$ as the chance the signal is real
Reporting the best of 40 specifications makes a small $p$ likely even with no signal
The abstract gives no effect size or confidence interval
$p = 0.004$ is too small to be believable
options.why: Small $p$-values happen with real effects and big samples. The problem is how this one was chosen.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because 0.004 is below 0.05
options.why: Being below 0.05 does not repair a reversed conditional or a best-of-40 choice.

feedback.correct: Reversed conditional, choosing after looking, no effect size.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each sentence of the abstract against what a $p$-value means.

explain.text: $p$ assumes no signal, so $1 - p$ is not the chance it is real. Choosing the best of 40 inflates the chance of a small $p$ by luck. Without an effect size and interval, a reader cannot tell if the signal is worth trading.

items.prose: A desk wants to know whether a new hedging rule cuts daily hedging cost. It can run both rules side by side on the same 40 days. Or it can run the new rule on 40 later days.
items.question: Which design and test give the most power for the same 40 days of each?

options.text: Run both on the same days and test the daily differences
Run the new rule on later days and use Welch's test
options.why: Later days bring different markets, which adds noise the comparison cannot remove.

options.text: Run both on the same days but use a pooled two-sample test
options.why: That treats paired days as independent, throwing away the shared noise and with it power.

options.text: Test each rule's cost against zero and compare the verdicts
options.why: Two separate verdicts do not test the difference between the rules.

feedback.correct: Same days and a paired test cancel the shared market noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which design lets the shared market noise cancel.

explain.text: Hedging cost swings with the market. On the same days both rules see the same swings, so the daily differences cancel them. A paired test on those differences has far more power than any comparison of separate days.
